second_order: making UBC marks with maps, coordinates and calls for help
theme_note: These codes hold together because participants turn the wish for a UBC mark into shared pixel work: recruiting helpers, making or importing designs, choosing dimensions and coordinates. Later Cairn and crest codes vary the object and move from proposing it to announcing it built.

second_order: playing April Fools with fake campus stories and identities
theme_note: These codes perform or disclose the room's own April Fool conduct rather than canvas work. Most sustain the SFU switch through fake institutional claims, redirected campus questions and copied CSS; others vary the play with Trump, Robert Gateman, Natural recursion and ShawnHate jokes.

second_order: helping neighbouring marks when a pixel can be spared
theme_note: These codes make shared-canvas help the practice: first answering calls for Canada and CAPU, then protecting or filling university and neighbour marks. What varies is whether UBC asks for help, gives it, or fits it around its own defence.

second_order: celebrating and showing what the room made
theme_note: These codes publicly mark a completion or make the work visible through a completion post, celebration or timelapse. They vary from the Cairn and crest being declared done to displaying a record of the work.

second_order: making r/place familiar through Microsoft Paint and the Cairn
theme_note: This practice explains the unfamiliar canvas through ordinary or local comparisons. One code calls it multiplayer Microsoft Paint; a later one compares repeated crest defence with engineers defending the Cairn.

second_order: working out borders and deciding whose pixels to leave alone
theme_note: These codes negotiate limits rather than merely sharing neighbour names: asking for peace, opposing a build or incursion, proposing where a mark can go, and later invoking agreements or apologising for crossings. What varies is who claims prior space and whether the answer is restraint, withdrawal or a reciprocal promise.

second_order: calling people in against attacks on the marks
theme_note: These codes turn claimed danger into urgent collective defence: declaring war, naming an attacker, asking for protection and insisting the logo is not finished. Later codes vary the threat among neighbouring groups and the void, without settling who initiated each border crossing.

second_order: automating defence with scripts and spare accounts
theme_note: These codes hold together because participants shift repeated repainting into scripts, bots and multiple accounts. They vary from sharing and testing a Python script to finding old accounts and running a defender on a Raspberry Pi.

second_order: stopping when placement closes and losing the excuse to procrastinate
theme_note: These codes explicitly register that pixel placement has ended. The practice varies between simply announcing closure and joking that the end removes the reason to avoid other work.

second_order: joking, mourning and asking to fix OBC
theme_note: These codes respond to the frozen result as a shared imperfect outcome: celebrating and renaming it OBC, mourning a missed final pixel, requesting a repaired poster image and retelling later pixel chaos. Pride, disappointment, repair-seeking and retrospective joking vary within the same post-close practice.
